To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a well developed collateral circulation is a strong prognostic indicator in patients with acute myocardinal infarction (AMI) and stable CAD, and is an indicator of reduced infarct size and improved left ventricular function in AMI patients, but is not a prognostic indicator of survival in patients with sub-acute myocardial infraction.

in patients with acute myocardium infarction, the presence of well developed collaterals reduces infarct extension, and that in patients with stable coronary artery disease, the presence of an extensive collateral circulation reduces all-cause mortality.

in patients with acute myocarditis, an extensive collateral circulation is associated with a reduced risk of death and of recurrent myocardial infarctions, and in patients with stable coronary artery disease, a high collateral grade is associated with a lower rate of cardiac events.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the coronary collateral circulation is an important determinant of the clinical course of CAD and its presence is associated with a more benign prognosis.

the coronary collateral circulation is an important prognostic factor in patients with CAD and that the prognostic impact of collaterals is more pronounced in patients with acute myocardium infarction than in patients with sub-acute or chronic myocardial infarct.

coronary collateral circulation is an important factor in the natural history of coronary artery disease.
the coronary collateral circulation is not a “luxury function” in the human coronary circulation, but a “survival function” with prognostic relevance for all patients suffering from CAD.
